arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Ms. Blatt argued for the sides that brought the case. She focused on the child's best interests. She stated the father had no legal rights under state law.
Mr. Kneedler argued for the opposing side. He started with the definition of an official parent. He argued this definition drives the entire legal analysis.
Mr. Clement argued that without federal law, the father has no rights. He stated the child would receive a best interests determination. He emphasized the clarity of state law.

Mr. Rothfeld argued the child's custody was not transferred without a best interest determination. He stated this is clear from the lower court decisions. He rejected the claim of a procedural violation.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of federal protections for Native American families. The core conflict involves the definition of a family under federal law. One side argues for a broad biological definition. The other side argues for a definition based on actual custody and care.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case argue federal law should not override state custody rules. They claim the father had no legal standing. They emphasize the child's best interests as the primary goal.
the opposing side argues federal law creates a special family definition. They claim biological ties trigger federal protections. They assert this prevents the breakup of Indian families.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Scalia asked if this situation breaks up an Indian family. He noted the federal statute uses an expansive phrase. He distinguished this from state law definitions.
Justice Sotomayor asked why a noncustodial parent with visitation rights is not a family. She questioned the reliance on state definitions. She suggested a federal meaning might be better.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the legal meaning of an Indian family. It determines when federal law overrides state custody decisions. It affects the rights of biological parents in adoption cases. It shapes the balance between child welfare and cultural preservation.
